title: On Trial before Felix
sum: Five days after Paul is brought to Caesarea, the high priest Ananias arrives with elders and a hired advocate, Tertullus. After flattering the governor Felix, Tertullus charges Paul with being a public pest who starts riots among Jews everywhere, a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and a man who tried to defile the temple. Paul answers point by point. He came to Jerusalem only twelve days before, to worship; no one saw him stirring up a crowd; the Asian Jews who started the trouble have not come. He admits one thing: he serves the God of his ancestors according to the Way, believes the Law and the Prophets, and shares Israel's hope that God will raise the righteous and the unrighteous.

Felix, who knows more about the Way than he lets on, adjourns the case and keeps Paul under easy guard. Later he and his wife Drusilla, a princess of the Herod family, send for Paul to hear about faith in Christ Jesus. When Paul speaks of justice, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix grows afraid and sends him away. He keeps hoping for a bribe, and when he leaves office two years later he leaves Paul in chains to please the Jewish leaders.
readings: Read as history

The cast fits what Josephus and Tacitus tell of Judea in the late 50s: a high priest known for greed, a governor born a slave who married a Herodian princess and dealt harshly with unrest, and a legal process in which charges of sedition counted most. Roman procedure shows through: a formal complaint, a hired advocate, the accused speaking in his own defense, an adjournment, custody with privileges, a governor hoping for money. Many historians judge the scene plausible in its details, whatever Luke has done with the speeches.
Read as Luke's story

Luke shapes Paul's trials to follow Jesus' trial and the apostles' (Luke 23; Acts 4–5): accusers from the Temple, charges of stirring up the people, a governor who sees no crime but will not set the prisoner free. He also uses the trials to say what Christians are: not rebels, but followers of the Way, faithful to Israel's God and Israel's hope. The real issue, Paul insists, is the resurrection.

views.H: Felix (governor about 52–59/60) is well documented. Josephus describes his harsh campaigns against bandits and the Egyptian prophet, his part in the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, and his marriage to Drusilla; Tacitus calls him a man who used a king's power with a slave's mind. The scene's legal details (formal accusation, absent witnesses, custody with relief) match Roman practice described by Sherwin-White and Rapske. The two years of custody before Festus' arrival (about 59–60) is a key date for Paul's chronology.
views.C: Critical scholars note how closely Luke's speeches follow the rules of Greek and Roman rhetoric, and conclude that Luke composed them, as ancient historians commonly did (Thucydides 1.22). Many see an apologetic purpose: Roman officials find Paul innocent, and the movement is presented as a lawful party within Judaism. The almost total silence about Paul's collection, mentioned only at 24:17, is often taken as a sign that Luke knew of a difficulty he chose not to tell.
views.L: The chapter is built as a pair of speeches, accusation and defense, followed by a private scene that turns the tables: the judge becomes the one who is judged. The Way, a sect, the resurrection of the dead and the God of the fathers are the themes Paul will repeat before Festus and Agrippa. Felix's fear and delay mirror Herod Antipas, who wanted to see Jesus but heard nothing that changed him (Luke 23:8–12).
views.J: Paul defends himself as a loyal Jew: he came to worship, to bring alms and offerings, and was ritually pure in the temple. He calls the Way a party within Israel, like the Pharisees and Sadducees, and his hope the hope of Israel. Jewish scholars (Segal, Fredriksen, Nanos) read this Paul as recognizably Jewish. Readers should also notice that "the Jews" in 24:9 means the delegation from Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole.
views.T: John Chrysostom preached on this chapter as a picture of a prisoner freer than his judge: Paul speaks of righteousness and judgment to the man who holds his life, and Felix trembles. Church teachers have used Felix's "Leave for now" (KJV "when I have a convenient season") as the classic example of putting off repentance. The chapter's statement of the resurrection of the just and the unjust (24:15) became a standard proof text for a general resurrection (see the card).

deep.h: The speeches in Acts: Paul's words or Luke's?
deep.b:
About a third of Acts is speeches, and this chapter has two. How close are they to what was said? Ancient historians openly wrote speeches for their characters. Thucydides says he kept "as closely as possible to the general sense of what was actually said" while making speakers say what the occasion required (History 1.22); many later historians were less careful.

  • Luke composed them. Martin Dibelius argued that the speeches are Luke's own, written to show the meaning of each moment to his readers. Their style is Luke's, and they share patterns across speakers. Most critical scholars hold some form of this view.
  • Summaries of real speeches. Others, such as F. F. Bruce, Colin Hemer and Craig Keener, argue that Luke worked like the better historians: he condensed what was said, sometimes from his own memory or reliable reports, in his own words. They point to features that fit the speaker and the setting, such as Tertullus' textbook flattery and Paul's legal points.

Both sides agree the speeches are summaries: Tertullus' speech takes about thirty seconds to read aloud. The question is how much of the substance goes back to the occasion.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the alms and the bribe
deep.b: Paul tells Felix he came to Jerusalem "to give alms for my people" (24:17), and two verses later Luke says Felix hoped Paul would give him money (24:26). Commentators have connected the two. I would go one step further: Luke's silence about the collection, which Paul's letters treat as the great purpose of this journey (Romans 15:25–31), may be because the collection became part of the legal trouble. A large sum of money from Gentile cities, brought to Jerusalem by a man accused of starting riots, could look to a Roman governor like funding for unrest, or like a source of profit for himself. If so, Luke leaves the collection out of the story and mentions it only in Paul's defense, where it shows his loyalty to his people. This is a guess built on two verses and on Luke's silence. It overlaps with suggestions by several scholars that the collection was received awkwardly or not at all.

settings.by: Tertullus, the advocate, speaking for the high priest Ananias and the elders
settings.to: Felix, the Roman governor, in the hearing at Herod's palace in Caesarea, with Paul present
settings.when: five days after Paul was sent to Caesarea under guard
settings.why: to win over the governor with praise and then frame Paul as a political danger: a plague, a starter of riots across the empire, the leader of a sect, and a temple defiler. Sedition was the charge Rome feared, so Tertullus leads with it; the temple charge was the one the priests could claim to judge themselves.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches he wrote for, faced the same accusation: that Christians were troublemakers who upset cities. The scene shows how the charge was first made and how weak it was.

settings.to: Felix, with Ananias, the elders and Tertullus present
settings.when: at the same hearing
settings.why: to answer each charge in turn: he was in Jerusalem only twelve days and caused no riot; he came to worship and to bring alms and offerings; the witnesses who claimed to see a crime are absent; and the only "crime" he admits is belonging to the Way and hoping in the resurrection, a hope he shares with his accusers. He turns a political charge back into a question of Jewish belief that a Roman court should not judge.
settings.readers: For Luke's churches, the speech models how to answer an accusation: with facts, courtesy, a clear conscience, and an open statement of faith. It also claims the Way's place within Israel.

settings.to: the accusers and Paul; then the centurion in charge of Paul
settings.when: at the end of the hearing
settings.why: to postpone a decision that would offend either the Temple leaders or Roman justice, under the pretext of waiting for Lysias, while keeping Paul in mild custody
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw a Roman official who could find no crime but would not act on it, as Pilate had done with Jesus.

settings.what: Paul speaks to Felix and Drusilla
settings.to: Felix and his wife Drusilla, a Jewish princess of the Herod family, in a private audience
settings.when: some days after the hearing
settings.why: Felix wanted to hear about faith in Christ Jesus. Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment: the demands of that faith, aimed at a corrupt judge who had taken another man's wife. The words were meant to call them to repentance; they frightened Felix instead.
settings.readers: A model of speaking the truth to the powerful, and a warning to readers against putting off a decision until "a better time."

traditions.q: Paul hopes for "a resurrection... of the righteous and the unrighteous alike" (24:15). Are all the dead raised together for judgment, and what happens to the unrighteous who are raised?
views: All the dead, righteous and unrighteous, will rise with their own bodies at Christ's return, in one general resurrection, for the Last Judgment; the righteous to eternal life, the wicked to eternal separation from God (Catechism 998–1001, 1033–1038).
At the end Christ will raise all the dead, give eternal life and joy to the godly, and condemn the ungodly "to be tormented without end" (Augsburg Confession XVII).

At the last day all the dead will be raised with the same bodies: the bodies of the unjust to dishonor, those of the just to honor, followed by a general judgment of all (Westminster Confession 32.3; 33.1–2).

There are two resurrections separated by the thousand years of Revelation 20: the righteous are raised at Christ's coming, the unrighteous after the millennium to stand before the great white throne. Acts 24:15 names both groups without saying they rise at the same time.

The righteous rise at the second coming; the wicked rise at the end of the millennium, are judged, and are destroyed by fire. Their punishment is final death, not endless torment, because human beings are not naturally immortal (Fundamental Beliefs 26–27).

Acts 24:15 is a key text: "the unrighteous" are people who died without knowing God's requirements. They will be raised to life on earth during Christ's thousand-year reign and given the chance to learn and obey. Those judged wicked beyond repentance are not raised at all.

Most evangelicals hold a general resurrection of all for judgment, with everlasting conscious punishment for the lost. A significant minority, including John Stott and Edward Fudge, have argued that the unrighteous are raised to be judged and then cease to exist.

title: I Appeal to Caesar
sum: A new governor, Porcius Festus, arrives and within three days goes up to Jerusalem. The chief priests renew their charges and ask him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, planning to ambush him on the road. Festus tells them to come to Caesarea instead. There the Jerusalem leaders bring many serious charges they cannot prove. Paul denies doing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul refuses: he is already before Caesar's court, and he appeals to Caesar. Festus, after consulting his advisers, accepts: "To Caesar you will go!"

Before Paul can be sent, King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice come to greet Festus. Festus tells the king about the strange case: no crime, only disputes about the Jews' religion and "one Jesus, who had died," whom Paul says is alive. Agrippa wants to hear Paul, and the next day, in a grand audience, Festus presents the prisoner to the king and the leading men of Caesarea. He admits he has nothing definite to write to the emperor.
readings: Read as Roman legal history

The chapter is a key text for Roman law in the provinces. A. N. Sherwin-White argued that its picture of a citizen's appeal before sentence, the governor's council, the duty to send a report, and the political pressures on a new governor fits the 50s and 60s, and not later practice. Even scholars who doubt other parts of Acts often credit Luke with accurate knowledge here.
Read as the turning point

Luke's story turns on 25:11. Paul has been promised that he will bear witness in Rome (23:11); now he chooses the road himself. From here to the end, the goal is fixed. The scene with Agrippa follows the pattern of Jesus' trial, where Pilate also sent the prisoner to a Herod (Luke 23:6–12).

views.H: Festus (about 59–62) is known from Josephus as a more energetic governor than Felix; his death in office left the gap in which the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus killed (about 62). Agrippa II (about 27–93/100) held lands in the north and authority over the temple and high priesthood; Bernice's later affair with Titus is reported by Tacitus and Suetonius. The procedures in the chapter (the bēma, the consilium, the appeal, the governor's report) agree with what is known of Roman law in the period.
views.C: Critical scholars ask whether a provincial citizen could really appeal before any verdict, and why Festus, who found no crime, did not simply acquit. Some suspect that Luke has shaped the account so that every Roman official declares Paul innocent. Others, following Sherwin-White, find the legal details too precise to be invented, and the governor's caution politically realistic. Festus' report to Agrippa (25:14–21) differs from what the narrator showed, a sign that Luke lets characters speak for themselves.
views.L: Luke builds the chapter on repetition: a second plot (25:3; compare 23:12–22), a second hearing with the same unproven charges, and a second report by a Roman official (compare Lysias' letter, 23:26–30). Festus' summary of the case, "one Jesus, who had died, and who Paul kept saying is alive," puts the gospel in the mouth of an outsider. The grand entry of Agrippa and Bernice sets up the long speech of chapter 26.
views.J: Paul again denies any offense against the Jewish law or the temple. The chief priests act as a political body seeking advantage with a new governor; Luke does not present the Jewish people as a whole here. Festus calls the dispute a matter of "their own religion," an outsider's view that turns a debate among Jews about the resurrection and the Messiah into a curiosity.
views.T: The appeal to Caesar has been read in the churches as a sign that Christians may use the protections of law and citizenship (see the note on 25:11). Paul's "I am not trying to get out of dying" was cited in older Christian teaching on the powers of the state. Patristic preachers such as Chrysostom contrasted Festus' confusion with the clarity of Paul's witness.

deep.b:
Luke tells the trials of Paul so that they echo the trial of Jesus in his Gospel. The parallels are clearest in chapters 21–26:

  • Both go up to Jerusalem knowing what waits there (Luke 9:51; 18:31–33; Acts 20:22–24; 21:10–14).
  • Both are seized by the Temple authorities' side and handed over to the Romans (Luke 22:54; 23:1; Acts 21:30–33; 28:17).
  • Both are struck or mocked before the high priest's court (Luke 22:63–64; Acts 23:2).
  • Both are charged with stirring up the people and opposing Caesar (Luke 23:2, 5; Acts 24:5; 25:8).
  • Both appear before a Roman governor and a Herod (Luke 23:1–12; Acts 24–26).
  • Both are declared innocent by the governor more than once (Luke 23:4, 14, 22; Acts 23:29; 25:25; 26:31–32).

The parallel is not complete: Paul is not crucified, and Acts does not tell his death. Charles Talbert and Robert Tannehill, among others, have studied these patterns. Readers differ on what they mean: a literary device, a theological claim that the disciple follows the master, or an apologetic case that Christians, like Jesus, were innocent before Roman law.

deep.h: Could a Roman citizen just appeal?
deep.b:
By old Roman law a citizen could appeal (provocatio) against a magistrate's power to flog or execute him. Under Augustus, the Julian law on public violence protected citizens who appealed, and the right became an appeal to the emperor. Paul's appeal comes before a verdict, which Sherwin-White saw as typical of the earlier empire; later, governors increasingly judged citizens themselves, though Pliny still sent citizen Christians to Rome about 112 (Letters 10.96).

Questions remain. How did Paul prove he was a citizen? Citizens could carry a folding tablet recording their birth registration, but Acts never says Paul showed one. Did the emperor hear such cases himself? Often he delegated them. What happened to Paul's case in Rome is unknown (see 28:30).

settings.to: the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews in Jerusalem
settings.when: on his first visit to Jerusalem, three days after taking office
settings.why: to keep the case at Caesarea, where Roman justice and his own control were secure, while seeming cooperative: their men with authority could come down and make their charges there
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw a Roman official, without knowing it, protect Paul from a murder plot.

settings.to: Festus on the judgment seat at Caesarea, with the Jerusalem accusers standing around
settings.when: at the formal hearing, the day after Festus returned
settings.why: to deny every kind of charge (Jewish law, temple, Caesar), to refuse a trial in Jerusalem that would put him at his enemies' mercy, and to claim his right as a citizen to be heard by the emperor. The appeal moved the case out of reach of the local politics.
settings.readers: For Christians accused before magistrates, the scene showed that a believer could use the protections of law with a clear conscience, and that God's purpose could work through them.

settings.to: Paul, after consulting his council
settings.when: at the end of the hearing
settings.why: to accept the appeal formally, which also freed Festus from an awkward decision
settings.readers: The words "To Caesar you will go" fix the goal of the rest of Acts.

settings.to: King Agrippa II and Bernice, privately, during their visit to Caesarea
settings.when: some days after the hearing
settings.why: to seek the help of an expert in Jewish affairs, and to present his own handling of the case in the best light. His summary shows how a Roman saw the dispute: a matter of Jewish religion and of a dead man named Jesus whom Paul said was alive.
settings.readers: Luke's readers heard the gospel summarized by an outsider who could not judge it, and saw how Roman officials described Christians.

settings.to: King Agrippa, Bernice, the military commanders and the leading men of Caesarea, in the audience hall
settings.when: the next day, at a formal gathering
settings.why: to explain why the hearing was being held: the whole Jewish people (as he put it) wanted Paul dead, he himself found no capital crime, and he needed something to write to the emperor
settings.readers: Another Roman verdict of innocence, delivered in public, for readers who needed to know that the faith was not a crime.

title: Before King Agrippa
sum: Given leave to speak, Paul makes the fullest defense of his life in Acts. He tells King Agrippa that all the Jews know he lived from his youth as a Pharisee, the strictest party of their religion, and that he is on trial for the very hope his people's twelve tribes pray for night and day: the promise God made to the fathers, which includes the raising of the dead. He admits that he once fought the name of Jesus with fury, jailing believers, voting for their deaths and hunting them in foreign cities.

Then he tells for the third time in Acts how, on the road to Damascus at midday, a light brighter than the sun threw him and his companions to the ground, and Jesus spoke to him in Hebrew: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? Kicking against the goads is hard on you." In this telling Jesus himself gives the commission: to be a witness, sent to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles and turn them from darkness to light. Paul obeyed, preaching repentance, and says he teaches only what Moses and the prophets foretold: a suffering Messiah, first to rise from the dead, bringing light to Israel and the nations.

Festus breaks in: Paul's learning has made him mad. Paul calmly answers that his words are true and sober, and turns to the king: "Do you believe the prophets?" Agrippa deflects: "With so little, you would talk me into making myself a Christian?" Paul wishes that everyone listening would become what he is, except for the chains. The officials withdraw and agree that Paul has done nothing worth death or prison; he could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar.
readings: Read as Paul's testimony

For many Christian readers this is Paul's own story in his own words: his zeal, his conversion, his mission. It sits beside his letters (Galatians 1:13–17; Philippians 3:4–11; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10), which agree on the main points: a persecutor, a Pharisee, called by the risen Jesus to the Gentiles.
Read as Luke's climax

Literary readers see the speech as the summit of Paul's defense in Acts: before a governor, a king and a city's nobility, Paul fulfills Jesus' words that his followers would testify before governors and kings (Luke 21:12–13; Acts 9:15). Luke gives Paul his most polished Greek and lets the scene end not with a verdict on Paul but with a question to the king.

views.H: Agrippa II's authority over the temple and his knowledge of Jewish affairs are well attested in Josephus. The proverb about the goads is Greek, not Hebrew or Aramaic, which some take as a sign that Luke shaped the words for a Greek audience. Festus' outburst, Agrippa's dry reply, and the private verdict of innocence are plausible in a hearing that was not a trial but an inquiry for the governor's report.
views.C: Critics compare the three accounts of Paul's call (9; 22; 26) and find differences in detail: who saw and heard what, whether Ananias was involved, where the commission came from. Some take the differences as Luke's free retelling for each audience; some as evidence that the speeches are Luke's compositions. Vielhauer and others contrast this Paul's message (repentance and works worthy of it) with the Paul of the letters (justification by faith); others answer that 26:18 names faith and that a defense speech is not a letter to a church.
views.L: The speech follows the shape of a formal defense: courteous opening, the speaker's past, the decisive event, his conduct since, and an appeal. Its key words, "hope," "promise," "raise," "light," "witness," gather up themes from all of Luke-Acts. The commission (26:16–18) echoes the calls of Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Isaiah's servant, and the Messiah's mission to be "light to the people and to the Gentiles" (26:23) echoes Simeon's song (Luke 2:32). The scene's open ending (Agrippa's question unanswered) anticipates the open ending of the book.
views.J: Paul presents himself throughout as a Jew: a Pharisee, sharing the hope of the twelve tribes, teaching only what Moses and the prophets said. Jewish scholars such as Alan Segal read his experience as a Jewish mystic's vision of the glorified figure of God's presence, and his call as a prophet's commission; Paula Fredriksen stresses that Paul never stopped being a Jew. The speech itself places the conflict inside Israel ("I am being accused, and by Jews!"), not between Jews and a new religion.
views.T: The church has read 26:18 as a summary of salvation: opened eyes, darkness to light, Satan to God, forgiveness, inheritance among the saints. The call scene is celebrated in the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul (25 January) in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran calendars. Agrippa's reply, through the KJV's "Almost thou persuadest me," became a fixture of revival preaching and hymns about the danger of being nearly but not fully converted.

deep.b:
Acts tells Paul's call three times: by the narrator (9:1–19), by Paul to a Jerusalem crowd (22:3–16), and by Paul to Agrippa (26:9–18). The shared Greek is translated the same way in all three on this site: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" "Who are you, Lord?" "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" (22:8 adds "the Nazarene," as the Greek does).

  • The light: it flashes "from heaven" (9:3); it comes "around midday" as "a powerful light" (22:6); here it outshines the sun at midday and shines on his companions too, and the verb changes: 9:3 and 22:6 say it "flashed" (periastraptō), 26:13 that it "shone" around them (perilampō).
  • The companions: they stand speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (9:7); they see the light but do not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9); they all fall to the ground (26:14).
  • The words: only 26:14 adds "in Hebrew" and "Kicking against the goads is hard on you."
  • The commission: given through Ananias, and told to Ananias rather than Paul (9:15–16); given through Ananias to Paul (22:14–15), with a later vision in the temple (22:17–21); given by Jesus himself on the road (26:16–18).

Harmonizers note that Greek "hear" can mean hearing a sound or understanding words, and that each account is shorter than the event. Many scholars think Luke deliberately varied the retellings: the Jerusalem crowd hears of the devout Jew Ananias; the king hears of a direct commission from heaven. Either way, Luke thought this story important enough to tell three times, as he told Peter's vision twice (10–11).

Was Paul converted, or called? Krister Stendahl argued in 1963 and in Paul among Jews and Gentiles (1976) that Paul's letters describe his experience as a prophet's call, not as a conversion from one religion to another or from a guilty conscience to peace. Paul never says he felt guilt as a Pharisee (Philippians 3:6), and he describes his call in the words of Jeremiah and Isaiah (Galatians 1:15). This chapter supports Stendahl's reading: the commission follows the pattern of prophetic calls.

Alan Segal, a Jewish scholar, answered that Paul did undergo a conversion in the full sense: he changed communities and reinterpreted his whole past. James Dunn and others hold both together: Paul was called to a mission, and the call turned his life around. The words of 26:18 apply "turn" to Paul's hearers, not to Paul himself.

echoes: Acts 9:1–19; Acts 22:3–16; Galatians 1:13–17; Philippians 3:4–11; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10; Ezekiel 2:1; Jeremiah 1:5–8; Isaiah 42:6–7; Isaiah 42:16; Isaiah 49:6; Luke 2:32; Luke 21:12–15; Luke 24:26–27; Luke 24:44–47; Deuteronomy 32:39

settings.to: King Agrippa II and Bernice, the governor Festus, the military commanders and the leading men of Caesarea, in the audience hall
settings.when: the day after Agrippa asked to hear him, at an inquiry held to help Festus write his report to the emperor
settings.why: to show a king learned in Jewish customs that Paul's message is the fulfillment of Israel's own hope; that his change from persecutor to witness came from a vision of the risen Jesus that he could not disobey; and that what he preaches is only what Moses and the prophets foretold. The speech defends Paul and invites the king to believe.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's churches, the speech gathers the whole message of Luke-Acts into one place: the resurrection as Israel's hope, the risen Jesus as the Messiah who suffered, and the mission to both Israel and the nations. It also answers the charge that Christianity was a new and lawless religion.

settings.what: Festus' outburst and the exchange with Agrippa
settings.to: one another, before the assembly
settings.when: as Paul reached the resurrection and the light to the Gentiles
settings.why: Festus' cry dismisses resurrection as madness; Paul's answer claims sober truth and public facts, and presses the king to confess what he believes about the prophets. Agrippa avoids the trap with irony, and Paul answers with a courteous wish for them all.
settings.readers: Luke's educated readers met the two common reactions to the gospel, scorn and polite evasion, and Paul's response to each.

settings.to: one another, after leaving the hall; then Agrippa to Festus
settings.when: at the end of the inquiry
settings.why: to agree privately that Paul was innocent of any crime deserving death or prison, and to note the irony that his appeal now prevented his release
settings.readers: A final verdict of innocence from a Roman governor and a Jewish king, the counterpart of Pilate's and Herod's verdicts on Jesus (Luke 23:13–15).

title: Storm and Shipwreck
sum: Paul and other prisoners sail for Italy under a centurion named Julius, with Aristarchus and the narrator ("we") on board. Coasting along Asia Minor against the summer winds, they change at Myra to an Alexandrian grain ship and struggle west to Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete. It is now after the Day of Atonement, and the sailing season is closing. Paul warns that going on will cost the cargo, the ship and lives, but the centurion trusts the helmsman and the shipowner, who want to reach a better harbor for the winter.

A gentle south wind tempts them out; then a hurricane-force northeaster sweeps down from the mountains of Crete. The ship is driven before it. The crew haul in the skiff, brace the hull with cables, let down the gear to avoid the sandbanks of Syrtis, and throw out cargo and tackle. For many days there is no sun and no stars, and all hope of being saved fades. Paul stands up among them: an angel of his God has told him he must stand before Caesar, and God has given him the lives of all who sail with him. They will run aground on an island, but no one will be lost.

On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adria, the sailors sense land. Soundings show shallowing water; they drop anchors from the stern and pray for day. Paul stops the sailors from slipping away in the skiff, and before dawn he urges everyone to eat, takes bread, gives thanks to God before them all, breaks it and eats. All 276 take heart. At daybreak they run the ship for a beach, but it sticks fast and the stern breaks up. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Some swim, others float on planks and wreckage, and all reach land safely.
readings: Read as an eyewitness account

Since James Smith's study in 1848, many sailors and historians have judged this the most detailed description of an ancient voyage to survive. The courses, winds, seasons, sailing terms and soundings fit what is known of the Mediterranean, and Smith showed that a ship drifting from Cauda would reach Malta in about fourteen days. For readers who take the "we" as Luke's own presence, this chapter is the strongest evidence.
Read as a story of salvation

Luke tells the rescue with the words of salvation ("saved," "rescue," "brought safely through"), and Paul, the prisoner, becomes the one through whom God saves everyone on board. The meal before dawn uses the words of the Last Supper. Many readers have seen in the chapter a parable of the church's mission: God's purpose to bring the gospel to Rome cannot be wrecked, and those who travel with God's servant are saved with him.
Read alongside ancient sea stories

Storms and shipwrecks were favorite scenes in Greek novels and histories, and Jonah's storm is the great biblical example. Some scholars (Robbins, Pervo) read Acts 27 in that literary setting, as a dramatic set piece. Others (Hemer, Keener) answer that literary skill does not rule out a real event: Josephus and Paul himself were shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:25), and Luke's details are uncommonly precise.

views.H: The route fits the season and the winds: east of Cyprus against the northwesterlies, the grain ship at Myra, Fair Havens and Phoenix on Crete, the Euraquilo off the mountains, the drift past Cauda toward the Syrtis and on across the Adria to Malta. Vegetius' dates for the sailing season, Claudius' incentives for grain shippers, Josephus' wreck in the Adria about AD 63, and Smith's measurements at St Paul's Bay all support the account's realism.
views.C: Martin Dibelius argued that Luke took a secular account of a voyage and inserted Paul's speeches (27:9–11, 21–26, 31, 33–36), noting that these verses could be removed without breaking the sea story. Others reply that Paul's actions are woven into the plot (the skiff, the meal, the centurion's motive). Vernon Robbins proposed that "we" was a convention of sea narratives; critics answered that many sea stories are in the third person. Pervo reads the chapter as a skilled adventure tale with a theological point.
views.L: The chapter is a turning of the tables: the prisoner advises the centurion, encourages the crew, presides at a meal, and is the reason everyone survives. Salvation words run through it (27:20, 31, 34, 43–44). Jonah lies behind it: a storm, sailors, cargo thrown out, a servant of God who confesses his God, and the Gentile sailors spared. The angel's "You have to stand before Caesar" (27:24) keeps the destination in view.
views.J: Luke dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar ("the Fast," the Day of Atonement). Paul acts as a pious Jew: he gives thanks to God before eating, as Jewish custom required at every meal. His confession of "the God who owns me, the God I worship" before pagan sailors recalls Jonah 1:9, and the deliverance from the sea recalls the psalms of those who go down to the sea in ships (Psalm 107:23–30).
views.T: John Chrysostom preached on Paul as the pilot of the ship in all but name, and on the 276 saved for one righteous man's sake. Church tradition has long read the ship as an image of the church carried through the world's storms. Whether the meal of 27:35 was a Eucharist has been debated since the early commentators; most have taken it as an ordinary meal blessed in thanksgiving. Malta's churches keep the shipwreck as their founding story (feast of St Paul's Shipwreck, 10 February).

deep.b:
Few chapters of the Bible have been checked so closely by experts outside theology. James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman and geologist, sailed the waters and studied Admiralty charts, publishing The Voyage and Shipwreck of St. Paul in 1848. He concluded that every detail of course, wind and timing was accurate, and that the wreck occurred at St Paul's Bay on Malta. William Ramsay, Colin Hemer and Brian Rapske built on his work.

On the other side, Dibelius saw a secular voyage account with Paul added; Pervo, a lively piece of fiction; Robbins, a literary convention. Even many skeptical scholars accept that the voyage itself reflects accurate knowledge of sailing. The debate is mainly over Paul's role in it: whether the speeches and the leading part he plays are Luke's additions.

Two details have drawn special attention: the 276 people aboard (a large ship, but smaller than Josephus' 600) and the depth soundings (twenty and fifteen fathoms), which match the approach to St Paul's Bay.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Jonah turned inside out
deep.b:
Many readers have noticed echoes of Jonah 1 in Acts 27. I think Luke built the chapter as a deliberate reversal of Jonah, and that the reversal carries his theology of the Gentile mission:

  • Jonah boards a ship fleeing God's call to preach to Gentiles; Paul boards a ship carrying him to preach in the Gentile capital.
  • Jonah sleeps in the storm while the pagans pray; Paul stands up and speaks while the pagans despair.
  • The sailors throw cargo, then Jonah, overboard to save themselves; here the cargo goes overboard, but Paul must stay, and the sailors must stay too (27:31), for anyone to be saved.
  • Jonah's sailors fear the LORD and offer sacrifice once the sea is calm; Paul's shipmates eat bread over which he has thanked God, and all are saved.
  • Jonah ends angry that God spared Gentiles; Acts ends with Paul announcing that salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (28:28).

If this is right, Acts 27 shows the reluctant prophet's story corrected: the servant of God who goes willingly to the nations brings salvation to everyone in the boat. This is my reading. It overlaps with published suggestions of Jonah parallels in commentaries (for example Pervo and Johnson), but the claim that Luke designed a point-by-point reversal is not one I can attribute to them.

echoes: Jonah 1:1–16; Psalm 107:23–30; Luke 8:22–25; Luke 21:18; Luke 22:19; Luke 24:30; 1 Samuel 14:45; Genesis 18:23–32; Acts 23:11; 2 Corinthians 11:25–26

settings.to: the centurion Julius, the helmsman, the shipowner and the others deciding whether to sail on
settings.when: at Fair Havens on Crete, after the Day of Atonement, as the sailing season closed
settings.why: to warn, from experience and insight, that sailing on would bring damage and loss of ship, cargo and lives. The warning was rejected, but it gave Paul authority later.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned to trust the word of God's servant over the confident experts, a theme that runs through the chapter.

settings.to: everyone on board, crew, soldiers and prisoners, most of them pagans, after many days without food
settings.when: in the height of the storm, when all hope of being saved was gone
settings.why: to restore hope: an angel of his God had promised that Paul would reach Caesar and that God had given him the lives of all on board. He told them to take heart, because the ship would be lost but not a life. The "I told you so" at the start was meant to win a hearing for the promise.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, the speech showed that God's purpose for the gospel to reach Rome could not be stopped by any storm, and that God's care reached the pagans who traveled with his servant.

settings.to: the centurion and the soldiers
settings.when: in the night, when the sailors tried to leave in the skiff
settings.why: to keep the crew on board, because the promise of rescue required everyone to stay together and the sailors were needed to beach the ship
settings.readers: God's promise did not make human action unnecessary: the promise was kept through good judgment and obedience.

settings.what: Paul urges them to eat, and gives thanks
settings.to: all 276 on board
settings.when: just before dawn on the fourteenth day
settings.why: to give them strength for the swim and the work ahead, to repeat the promise that not a hair would be lost, and by giving thanks to God over the bread in front of them all, to show where the rescue would come from
settings.readers: Christian readers heard the words of the Lord's Supper in the scene, whatever kind of meal it was, and saw Paul acting as host and pastor to a ship of strangers.

title: Rome, and an Open Door
sum: Safe on shore, the castaways learn they are on Malta. The islanders, who speak no Greek, welcome them with unusual kindness and build a fire against the rain and cold. A viper fastens on Paul's hand; the islanders decide he must be a murderer whom Justice will not let live, but when he shakes it into the fire and nothing happens they decide he is a god. The island's chief man, Publius, hosts them; Paul heals his father of fever and dysentery, and the island's sick come and are cured. After three months they sail on an Alexandrian ship to Puteoli, where believers welcome them, and walk to Rome. Believers come out along the Appian Way to meet Paul, and he takes heart.

In Rome Paul lives under guard in his own lodging. He calls the leaders of the Jewish community and tells them he has done nothing against his people or their customs; he wears his chain for the hope of Israel. They have heard nothing against him, but they know the sect is spoken against everywhere. On an appointed day many come, and from morning to evening he testifies to the kingdom of God and argues about Jesus from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some refuse. As they leave, divided, Paul quotes Isaiah 6: this people's heart has grown dull. God's salvation, he says, has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen. For two whole years Paul welcomes everyone who comes, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ openly, and no one stops him. There the book ends.
readings: Read as fulfillment

Jesus sent his witnesses to the end of the earth (1:8), and the Lord told Paul he must bear witness in Rome (23:11). The book ends with the gospel preached openly in the capital of the world. On this reading the ending is complete: the story Luke set out to tell, how the word went from Jerusalem to Rome, is finished.
Read as an open ending

Others notice what is missing: Paul's trial, his fate, the reaction of the emperor. The last scene with the Jews of Rome is divided, not final, and the last word is "unhindered." Daniel Marguerat and others read the open ending as an invitation: the story of the word continues in the readers' own time, and Israel's story is not closed.
Read with the Jewish people in mind

The ending's quotation of Isaiah 6 and the turn to the Gentiles have been read as God's final rejection of the Jews, and used that way in Christian teaching. Many scholars today read it differently: some Jews believed, Paul calls his chain "Israel's hope," and he goes on welcoming "everyone." How to read 28:25–28 is one of the main questions of Luke-Acts (see the deep dive and the card).

views.H: Malta's Punic-speaking population, the title "first man of the island" attested in inscriptions, the Alexandrian grain route to Puteoli, the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns on the Appian Way, and the custody of a prisoner awaiting trial in his own lodging with a soldier all fit the period. Rome's Jewish community was large and organized in many synagogues. What happened to Paul after the two years is not known from Acts; early tradition places his death in Rome under Nero (see the note on 28:30).
views.C: Why does Acts stop here? Some (Harnack, J. A. T. Robinson) think it was written about 62, before Paul's trial ended. Most critical scholars date Acts later and think Luke knew of Paul's death (foreshadowed in 20:25, 38) but chose to end on the triumph of the word. The Jewish leaders' ignorance of Paul (28:21) and the absence of the Roman church from the final scene puzzle some; others note that the believers who came to meet Paul (28:15) are the Roman church. The final turn to the Gentiles is read by some critics as Luke's verdict on the Jewish people (Sanders, Haenchen).
views.L: The book ends where its main lines meet: the kingdom of God (1:3; 28:23, 31), the witness to the end of the earth (1:8), Isaiah's word about seeing and not perceiving (Luke 8:10; Acts 28:26–27), the salvation of God seen by all flesh (Luke 2:30; 3:6; Acts 28:28). Luke shortened Isaiah 6 in his Gospel and saved the full quotation for here. The last word, "unhindered," closes a book full of hindrances. Rome's welcome on the Appian Way and Malta's kindness show Gentiles receiving Paul as the Jewish leaders divide.
views.J: Paul calls the Jewish leaders "brothers" and insists he has done nothing against his people; his chain is for "Israel's hope." The response is divided, as it was everywhere (13:43–45; 14:1–2; 17:4–5). Jervell argued that for Luke a divided Israel is the restored Israel of believers plus the hardened rest. Jewish and Christian scholars after the Holocaust have examined how 28:25–28 was used to teach that God had abandoned the Jews, and have read the passage against that history.
views.T: The church has read Malta's welcome and the healings as the first fruits of the gospel there; Malta, like Rome, honors Paul as its founder in faith. The arrival in Rome is linked in tradition with Peter's ministry and both apostles' martyrdoms there, commemorated together on 29 June. The final turn to the Gentiles shaped centuries of teaching about the church and Israel, a teaching the Catholic Church and many Protestant churches have revised since 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4).

deep.b:
Readers have long been surprised that Acts ends without telling the result of Paul's appeal. The main explanations:

  • Luke wrote before the outcome. Acts was finished about 62, while Paul waited in Rome (Harnack; J. A. T. Robinson). This explains the silence but sits uneasily with the common view that Luke's Gospel used Mark and was written after 70.
  • Luke knew, and chose not to tell. Paul's death is foreshadowed in his farewell (20:25, 38) and Agabus' prophecy (21:11). Ending with the word preached "unhindered" in Rome was more fitting for Luke's purpose than ending with an execution. Most scholars hold some form of this view.
  • Luke planned a third volume. Ramsay suggested it; there is no other evidence.
  • The ending is a literary choice. Marguerat and others argue that the open ending invites readers to carry on the story: the word is not chained, and its course continues beyond the book.

What later tradition says about Paul's last years is in the note on 28:30.

deep.h: Israel at the end of Luke-Acts
deep.b:
Paul turns to the Gentiles three times in Acts (13:46; 18:6; 28:28), each time after Jewish opposition, and the last time the book ends. Scholars have read this in very different ways:

  • A final rejection. Jack T. Sanders argued that Luke-Acts portrays the Jews as a people who rejected their salvation and are now outside it; Ernst Haenchen read 28:28 as Luke's farewell to Jewish mission.
  • A divided Israel. Jacob Jervell argued that for Luke the Jewish believers are restored Israel, and the Gentiles are added to them; the unbelieving part has excluded itself, but Israel has not been replaced.
  • A tragic story with an open future. Robert Tannehill read Luke-Acts as the tragedy of Israel: the hope announced in Luke 1–2 is not yet realized for most of the people, but the story is not over, and Paul still welcomes "everyone" (28:30).
  • Ambivalence. Joseph Tyson found both positive and negative images of Judaism throughout, with a darker turn toward the end.

Whatever Luke meant, the passage was used for centuries to support the teaching that God had rejected the Jews. Many churches have since rejected that teaching (see the card).

deep.title: Claude's theory: Nazareth and Rome
deep.b:
Luke's account of Jesus' ministry begins in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–30), and Acts ends in Paul's lodging in Rome. I think Luke built these two scenes as a frame:

  • Both open with the Scriptures read and explained to a Jewish audience (Luke 4:17–21; Acts 28:23).
  • Both quote Isaiah: Isaiah 61 on sight for the blind at Nazareth; Isaiah 6 on eyes that will not see in Rome.
  • Both audiences are at first open, then divided or hostile (Luke 4:22, 28; Acts 28:24–25).
  • Both end with God's mercy reaching Gentiles: the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:25–27); "this salvation from God has been sent out to the Gentiles" (Acts 28:28).
  • At Nazareth Jesus passes through the crowd and "went on his way" (Luke 4:30); in Rome the word goes on, and no one stops it (28:31).

If so, the end of Acts tells Luke's readers that what happened in Rome is what Jesus foresaw from the start: the gospel offered first to Israel, refused by many, and carried on to the nations, without God's purpose for Israel being withdrawn. The link between Luke 4 and Acts 28 has been noted by several scholars (for example Tannehill); the full list of parallels is my own arrangement.

echoes: Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:39–40; Romans 11:7–10; Luke 2:30–34; Luke 3:6; Isaiah 40:5; Psalm 67:2; Psalm 91:13; Luke 10:19; Mark 16:18; Acts 1:3; Acts 1:8; Acts 13:46; Acts 18:6; Acts 19:21; Acts 23:11; Romans 1:8–15; Romans 15:22–29; Philippians 1:12–14

settings.what: Paul to the Jewish leaders of Rome
settings.to: the leaders of Rome's synagogues, gathered at his lodging
settings.when: three days after he arrived in Rome
settings.why: to introduce himself before any rumor did, to explain that he came as a prisoner not by any fault against his people or their customs, and that he had appealed to Caesar not to accuse his nation but because he had no other choice; above all, to say that his chain was for Israel's hope. He wanted to be heard as a Jew among Jews.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw Paul end his ministry as he began it in every city: going first to the Jewish community, and presenting the faith as Israel's hope fulfilled.

settings.by: the leaders of the Jews in Rome
settings.to: Paul
settings.when: at the same meeting
settings.why: to say, carefully, that they had no reports against him and wished to hear his views, while noting that the sect was spoken against everywhere. Their reply keeps open both courtesy and caution.
settings.readers: The reply shows Rome's Jews as open to hearing, not hostile, which matters for how the final scene is read.

settings.what: Paul's day of teaching and his final word
settings.to: a larger group of Rome's Jews, at his lodging
settings.when: on an appointed day, from morning to evening
settings.why: to testify to the kingdom of God and persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. When they divided, he applied Isaiah 6 to those who refused, as a warning in the words of their own prophet, and announced that God's salvation had been sent to the Gentiles, who would listen.
settings.readers: For Luke's mostly Gentile churches, the scene explained why the church was now largely Gentile while remaining rooted in Israel's Scriptures. How far it closes the door on the Jewish people is debated (see the deep dive).
views: Sanders and Haenchen read 28:25–28 as Luke's last word on the Jewish people: they have refused, and the mission now belongs to the Gentiles.
Jervell and others note that some believed (28:24); the believing part of Israel is the restored people, and the warning applies to those who refused.
Tannehill reads the ending as tragic but not closed: Paul goes on welcoming "everyone" (28:30), and the healing Isaiah held out is still God's to give.

settings.to: the readers of Acts
settings.when: after two years of Paul's custody in Rome
settings.why: to close the book on the gospel preached openly and without hindrance in the capital of the empire, the goal set in 1:8 and 23:11
settings.readers: Theophilus and Luke's churches, who may have known more of Paul's fate than Luke tells (or, if Acts was written in the early 60s, did not yet know it), were left with the image of the word unchained, and with the story carried on into their own time.

traditions.q: Paul's last words in Acts apply Isaiah's hardening to Rome's Jews and say God's salvation "has been sent out to the Gentiles" (28:25–28). Has God turned away from the Jewish people?
views: No. The Jews remain "most dear" to God, "for God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:28–29); they must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839). The church still hopes for the day when all peoples will call on the Lord with one voice.

There is no single Orthodox statement like Nostra Aetate. The fathers most read in the Orthodox churches, above all John Chrysostom in his sermons against Judaizing Christians (Antioch, 386–387), spoke harshly of the Jews and treated their unbelief as having cost them their place, and some Holy Week hymns blame "the Jews" for the crucifixion. Many Orthodox theologians now distance themselves from that language; academic meetings between Orthodox and Jewish scholars have been held since the 1970s, and some Orthodox writers have asked for the hymns to be revised.

Luther in his late writings treated Jewish unbelief as a sign that God had abandoned the Jews and urged harsh measures against them. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) and other Lutheran bodies have repudiated those writings, and many Lutheran teachers today, reading Romans 11, deny that God has cast off the Jewish people.

There is one people of God, and the church of Jews and Gentiles is its continuation; Israel's unbelief is partial and temporary. Many Reformed teachers, following Romans 11:25–26, have expected a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ, and the Westminster Larger Catechism prays for "the Jews called" (Q. 191).

Israel and the church are distinct, and God's promises to national Israel still stand. Acts 28 marks the end of the offer of the kingdom to Israel in this age, not its cancellation; Israel will be restored as a nation at Christ's return. (A minority, the "Acts 28" dispensationalists such as E. W. Bullinger, date the start of the present church age from this very passage.)

Most evangelicals hold that salvation for Jews as for Gentiles comes through faith in Jesus, and support mission to Jewish people; many also expect a future large turning of Israel (Romans 11:26). Evangelicals differ on whether the church is the new Israel or a people alongside Israel.

traditions.q: On Malta Paul healed Publius' father by prayer and laying on of hands, and then all the island's sick (28:8–9). Do gifts of healing like this continue in the church today?
views: Yes. Divine healing is provided for in Christ's atonement and is the privilege of all believers; gifts of healing and prayer with laying on of hands continue as in Acts (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths 12).

God still heals. The church prays for the sick and celebrates the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (James 5:14–15), which may restore health if it serves the soul's salvation; charisms of healing are recognized, and miracles are investigated in the causes of saints (Catechism 1508–1513).

Healing belongs to the church's life: the sacrament of Holy Unction is offered for healing of soul and body, and miracles of healing are attributed to the prayers of the saints, to icons and to relics.

Many Reformed theologians are cessationists: the miraculous gifts were signs given to confirm the apostles' message and ceased with them (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, 1918). God still heals in answer to prayer, but not through people who have a gift of healing. Some Reformed churches are continuationist and disagree.

Baptists are divided: many follow a cessationist view like Warfield's, while others, especially in Africa, Asia and Latin America, expect gifts of healing today. Most practice prayer for the sick, sometimes with anointing (James 5:14–15).
